chapter: Luck, tricks and the Bourbon Street job
title: Lucky and unlucky dance-hall owners across the river
summary: Two owners with a Walkerstown place, and an Italian owner who sold out in a sugar sack of coins to a Black man whose business then thrived.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: He won. Just because it was his banjo. Well sure, that was just luck. I mean, there's a lot of luck there sometimes. It's not luck. You see, I tell you Mr. Bin, now you hear a lot of people say about luck. You take like this man's pick. That's the luckiest man in dancing, you know what I mean? I mean for business, you know what I mean? He was a lucky man for that, you see? And he, him and a colored fella had a place there over there in Walkerstown, you see? But this fella went fooling around and did wrong. He killed his wife, you see?

But he would have been a rich negro today Mr. Bin. He'd been rich. So, alright, yeah. Sent him up the river, you see? Well them two people were the luckiest people for business over on that side of the river. Yeah. You hear me for doing business. This fella, this colored fella, he had a place, was a block long. And he had music boxing of his own, you know what I mean? You see that you'd go in there, me and you go in there? You don't have to put nothing in the box.
He put it in the cell.

He asked you what number you like, you know what I mean? And he put it on. And he had a little grocery store too. See, and he was making money here over here. See? Alright. He turns around. A fella we used to play for back there, they called Loi, Loi Bartamana, an Italian fella. Now you talk with a bad luck man. Now he was bad luck for. He had this place, he was running this place, we used to play for him. He couldn't do no best with that place. You know why? Because he was a fella who couldn't take nothing. You understand me? You see you're in the village, you got a lot to take Mr. Bin. Yeah. So, what he did, he sold out. You know, he sold the binnets out to this Cullis fella. So this Cullis fella bought the binnets. So now look, when the fella came to buy the binnets out, he bought one of them sugar sacks, that much money in a sugar sack. And look, how you think he had the money in there? He had everything, pennies, nickels, dime, quarters, everything all man up in there now. Now you gotta sort all that out. Now look, he thinks this fella, because that fella had his money in that sack, that fella was a fool. You know what the Cullis fella told? He said, look, look, we, we, we, we, we, we not gonna count this money here. We going to the courthouse. And listen, the fella in the courthouse, I know that boy, I been knowing that boy when he was a little bit of a kid. You know what he told us? He said it must have took them a whole day to sort of that money out. You know what I'm talking about? He knew how much he had about it, did he? He madman didn't know the devil he had in that sack. Well he didn't even know. Because you know what he do? You see like you be playing for him. Yeah. He go in the register, when the register gets full, he just take all the money and just dump it in that sack and, you know, and tie it in. Yeah. He never leave no money ready. You know what he do? He boil it up and throw it on the counter. That's how he used to handle money. Yeah, because if there'd be a hold up, they wouldn't know where it was. That's right. So all right. So he bought this fella out. And Mr. Bill, I wouldn't tell you a word of a lie. That color fella bought that Italian fella business out. He used to give things Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. And Mr. Bill, I don't know why the people came for him. Something like that. Yeah. And you know what that Italian fella said? He said, well, I'll be John Brown. I don't see how he does it. I said, that's luck. See? And that fella know how to treat people. Yeah, that's right.
